content: The proportion of participants who discontinued the trial prematurely for any reason was utilized as an indicator of treatment tolerability. Search Strategy A comprehensive bibliographic database search was conducted using the Ovid interface. The databases included MEDLINE, MEDLINE In-Process, Embase, HMIC, PsycINFO, ASSIA, and CINAHL. This initial broad search aimed to identify not only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of interest but also other study methodologies and journal reviews related to pharmacotherapy for PTSD. The search terms were developed by combining previous strategies from NICE, Stein, and Australian Guideline reviews with an updated list of medications. Additional searches were performed to identify international studies in Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, and Portuguese, but no additional studies were identified. Furthermore, the National PTSD Centre’s PILOTS Database, the Cochrane Library, the Controlled Trials Register, Web of Knowledge, OpenSIGLE, and Google Scholar were searched using terms such as “post-traumatic stress disorder,” “PTSD,” “treatment,” “medication,” “pharmacotherapy,” and “controlled.” Reference lists of all selected studies and reviews were also scrutinized for additional RCTs. Study Selection One reviewer transferred the initial search results into EndNote X4 software, where duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of identified RCTs. Irrelevant studies were excluded, and potentially relevant studies were assessed for inclusion based on full texts. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion and guidance from a third senior reviewer. Data Extraction and Risk of Bias Assessment One reviewer extracted study details into a standardized format, which was then checked by another reviewer. Data collected included study citation, year of publication, location, setting, number of centers, design, sample size, duration, follow-up length, diagnostic criteria, inclusion/exclusion criteria, participant characteristics (e.g., gender distribution, age, PTSD symptom duration, comorbid depression, trauma type, randomization details, dropouts), intervention characteristics (e.g., mean and maximum doses), and outcome measures (e.g., intention-to-treat or completers-only samples). For intention-to-treat samples, the method of imputation was noted. Outcome data were entered into the Cochrane Collaboration’s Review Manager 5 software and cross-checked by another reviewer. Data from studies included in previous systematic reviews were also extracted and independently cross-checked for accuracy. Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Collaboration’s domain-based evaluation method, which considers random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants/personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources of bias. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and arbitration by a third senior rater. Masked study assessment (e.g., hiding journal or author details) was not undertaken, as its impact on bias reduction is unclear. Data Analysis Data synthesis was performed using Review Manager 5 software, employing meta-analysis techniques and generating forest plots for dichotomous and continuous data. Confidence intervals (CIs) of 95% were used for all analyses. Categorical outcomes, such as early study withdrawal, were analyzed using relative risk (RR) calculations, while continuous data were analyzed using standardized mean differences (SMD). Heterogeneity between studies was calculated using the I² statistic. A fixed-effects model was used when I² was less than 30%, indicating mild heterogeneity, while a random-effects model was applied for I² greater than 30%. Data were analyzed from the intention-to-treat sample in an “once randomized, always analyzed” manner to minimize bias from completers-only analyses. Results No RCTs of pharmacotherapy for children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress were identified. Evidence to Recommendation Benefits There is no evidence regarding the effects of benzodiazepines or antidepressants on symptom severity, functioning, or the presence of disorder in children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress. Harms There is no evidence on the adverse effects of benzodiazepines or antidepressants in this population. Observational and epidemiological studies in adults highlight risks of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal symptoms with benzodiazepines. NICE UK notes that chronic benzodiazepine use often leads to tolerance, limited therapeutic benefit, dependence (10–30% of chronic users), and withdrawal symptoms (50% of users). Limited studies in children and adolescents report similar dependency risks. Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, depression, nausea, and perceptual changes. Benzodiazepines are also associated with abuse potential, as they enhance and prolong the effects of other drugs and alleviate withdrawal symptoms. For antidepressants, evidence from children with depression highlights safety and tolerability concerns, including increased risk of suicidal ideation and behavior with some SSRIs. Tricyclic antidepressants are not recommended for children and adolescents. No data are available on the long-term consequences of psychotropic drug exposure in this population. Values and Preferences Children and adolescents, still in developmental stages, should only be exposed to drugs if other effective treatment options have been tried, the condition is severe, and treatment is likely to result in substantial improvement. Information on long-term consequences should also be available. Providing medication for acute stress may medicalize normal psychological reactions and contribute to dependence. Feasibility Training is required to ensure the safe administration of psychotropic medications and proper assessment of acute stress in children and adolescents, considering cultural variations. In many lowand middle-income countries, the continuous availability of psychotropic drugs in non-specialized healthcare settings is a challenge. Benzodiazepines and generic antidepressants are associated with low acquisition costs. Fluoxetine is included in the WHO list of essential medicines for treating depressive disorders in adolescents aged 8 years and older. Amitriptyline and diazepam are included in the Interagency Emergency Health Kit for primary healthcare needs in humanitarian emergencies. Final Recommendation Benzodiazepines and antidepressants should not be offered to reduce acute traumatic stress symptoms associated with significant impairment in daily functioning in children and adolescents. Strength of recommendation: strong. Quality of evidence: very low. Psychological first aid should be considered for children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress symptoms in the first month after a potentially traumatic event.
